summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while the territory legislates locally on many domestic matters. The result is a mixed record: the protections that visitors would rely on are national French provisions that apply here, and no source in this inventory records any local ordinance narrowing them.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies as French law; France's first wedding under that statute was reported on 29 May 2013, and the bill had been announced for introduction in Parliament in October 2012 as a campaign commitment. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual identity became prosecutable under the French Penal Code through the 2012 sexual-harassment legislation, and that provision was reworded to read gender identity in 2016. As a penal provision it extends to New Caledonia, so discriminatory conduct and transphobic motivation can be pursued as discrimination rather than as a distinct offence.

Detention is the sharpest documented risk. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code places prisoners according to their legal gender marker, so trans women are ordinarily held in all-male facilities where assault by other detainees is reported, placement following the identity document rather than anatomy. The French detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on-site inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. The French prison framework governs establishments in this collectivity, so the placement rule and the recorded pattern of violations apply here.

The overall assessment is therefore one of formal protection under an inherited national framework combined with a documented, unresolved vulnerability in custody. This record is evidence-thin on local conditions: it establishes what the law says and what the national machinery has found, and does not establish how those provisions are experienced on the ground in a small, close-knit society.
tangentialFactors:
The dating of the French measures is worth holding together: the marriage bill was announced in August 2012 for an October 2012 introduction, the sexual-identity discrimination ground entered the Penal Code in July 2012, the first same-sex wedding took place in May 2013, and the wording was updated to gender identity in 2016. These are French legislative acts extended to this collectivity rather than locally enacted steps.

The CGLPL material is drawn entirely from mainland French establishments, and its inspection sample is small: nine transgender detainees interviewed across four prisons. It evidences a systemic finding by the national oversight body rather than a measurement of conditions inside New Caledonian facilities specifically.

The BuzzFeed account of placement and assault exposure rests on reporting about French prisons in 2018 and describes the general mechanism of Article D248 rather than incidents in this territory. Read alongside the CGLPL opinion it indicates the direction of risk for a trans visitor remanded or sentenced here, not an incident count.
localsOnly:
Residents of New Caledonia may marry a partner of the same sex under the French statute extended to the territory, and the Penal Code ground covering sexual identity, reworded as gender identity in 2016, gives a basis for prosecuting discrimination, including discriminatory conduct motivated by transphobia.

People held in the territory's correctional facilities are placed according to the gender marker on their identity documents under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, which means trans women are generally assigned to all-male facilities regardless of anatomy or of how they live outside custody.

Trans detainees fall within the scope of the CGLPL's 2021 finding of persistent serious violations of rights in French places of deprivation of liberty, and may bring complaints to that watchdog as an oversight body with jurisdiction over French establishments.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Congrès of New Caledonia has adopted its own anti-discrimination or hate-crime ordinance addressing gender identity, and whether any such local instrument differs from the French Penal Code provision. The inventory does not address this.

Unresolved: the procedure and availability for changing a gender marker on French identity documents as applied in this collectivity, including whether a court order is required and which court handles it. No source in the inventory covers document amendment.

Unresolved: conditions inside New Caledonian prisons and detention centres specifically. Both the CGLPL opinion and the BuzzFeed reporting concern mainland French establishments, and neither reports an inspection or case in this territory.

Not sourced: entry, visa and border-screening practice for trans travellers arriving here, availability of gender-affirming care, access to gendered facilities, and any recorded incidents of violence against trans people in New Caledonia.
